subject: Physics
title: Second Law of Thermodynamics and Entropy Change
formulaOrRule: \Delta S = \int \frac{dq_{rev}}{T}, \quad \Delta S_{univ} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} \ge 0
derivationOrExplanation: Rudolf Clausius (1865) proved that for any reversible cyclic process, $\oint \frac{dq_{rev}}{T} = 0$, establishing that $dS = \frac{dq_{rev}}{T}$ is an exact differential of a state function. At reversible equilibrium, $\Delta S_{univ} = 0$.

title: Entropy Change of an Ideal Gas
formulaOrRule: \Delta S_{ideal\_gas} = n C_v \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) + n R \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = n C_p \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) - n R \ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)

subject: Physics
title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity Criterion
formulaOrRule: \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S, \quad \Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ} < 0 \text{ (Spontaneous)}
derivationOrExplanation: At constant $T$ and $P$, heat transferred to surroundings is $q_{surr} = -q_{sys} = -\Delta H_{sys}$. Surrounding entropy change is $\Delta S_{surr} = \frac{q_{surr}}{T} = -\frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Universal entropy change is $\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} = \Delta S_{sys} - \frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Multiplying by $-T$: $-T\Delta S_{univ} = \Delta H_{sys} - T\Delta S_{sys}$. Defining Gibbs free energy $G = H - TS$ gives $\Delta G_{sys} = -T\Delta S_{univ}$. Since $\Delta S_{univ} > 0$ for spontaneity, $\Delta G_{sys} < 0$.

title: Boltzmann Entropy Formula and Third Law
formulaOrRule: S = k_B \ln \Omega, \quad S(T=0) = 0 \quad (\text{Third Law of Thermodynamics})

variablesOrTerms.\\Omega: Number of accessible microstates corresponding to macroscopic state

derivationOrExplanation: Ludwig Boltzmann (1877) proved entropy is a logarithmic measure of microscopic multiplicity: $S = k_B \ln\Omega$. title: General Thermodynamic Heat Capacity Difference
formulaOrRule: C_p - C_v = T \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{T V \beta^2}{\kappa_T}
derivationOrExplanation: Internal energy differential is $dU = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V dT + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T dV$. Dividing by $dT$ at constant $P$ and noting $dH = dU + P\,dV + V\,dP$: $C_p - C_v = \left[P + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T\right]\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$. Using Maxwell relation $\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V - P$, the $P$ terms cancel, yielding $C_p - C_v = T\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{TV\beta^2}{\kappa_T}$. For ideal gas ($PV = nRT$), $\beta = 1/T$ and $\kappa_T = 1/P$, recovering Mayer's relation $C_p - C_v = R$.

title: Wave Speed on Stretched String and Laplace Formula for Sound
formulaOrRule: v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} \quad (\text{String}), \quad v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma R T}{M}} \quad (\text{Sound / Laplace})
derivationOrExplanation: For string: consider small curved pulse arc $ds$ of radius $R$: net centripetal tension component is $2T\sin(\Delta\theta/2) \approx T\Delta\theta = T(ds/R)$. Mass of element is $dm = \mu\,ds$. Centripetal equation is $T\frac{ds}{R} = dm \frac{v^2}{R} = (\mu\,ds)\frac{v^2}{R} \implies v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$. For sound: Newton assumed isothermal compression ($v = \sqrt{P/\rho}$), which underpredicted speed by 15%. Laplace corrected this: sound vibrations are so rapid that no heat exchanges occur, making process adiabatic ($B = \gamma P$), giving $v = \sqrt{\gamma P / \rho} = \sqrt{\gamma RT / M}$.

title: Doppler Effect for Acoustic Waves
formulaOrRule: f_{observed} = f_0 \left(\frac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}\right)

title: Beat Frequency
derivationOrExplanation: Superposition of two waves of equal amplitude: $y(t) = A\cos(2\pi f_1 t) + A\cos(2\pi f_2 t) = 2A\cos\left(2\pi\frac{f_1 - f_2}{2}t\right)\cos\left(2\pi\frac{f_1 + f_2}{2}t\right)$. title: Hohmann Transfer Orbit Velocity Impulse
formulaOrRule: \Delta v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r_1}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{2r_2}{r_1 + r_2}} - 1\right)

variablesOrTerms.r_1, r_2: Initial and target circular orbit radii

derivationOrExplanation: Semi-major axis of transfer ellipse is $a = \frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}$. Subtracting initial circular speed $v_1 = \sqrt{GM/r_1}$ yields $\Delta v$.

title: Gravitational Potential Inside a Solid Uniform Sphere
formulaOrRule: V_{in}(r) = -\frac{GM}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2) \quad (r \le R)
derivationOrExplanation: $V_{in}(r) - V(R) = -\int_R^r g(r')dr' = -\int_R^r \left(-\frac{GM}{R^3}r'\right)dr' = \frac{GM}{R^3}\left[\frac{r'^2}{2}\right]_R^r = \frac{GM}{2R^3}(r^2 - R^2)$. Since surface potential is $V(R) = -\frac{GM}{R} = -\frac{2GMR^2}{2R^3}$, we get $V_{in}(r) = -\frac{GM}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)$.

formulaOrRule: W = \int_{\vec{r}_1}^{\vec{r}_2} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int (F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz)

title: Conservative Force as Potential Energy Gradient
formulaOrRule: \vec{F} = -\vec{\nabla} U = -\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: By definition, work done by conservative force in differential displacement is $dW = -dU = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz$. From multivariable calculus, $dU = \frac{\partial U}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial U}{\partial z}dz$. Equating coefficients yields $F_x = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}$, $F_y = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial y}$, $F_z = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}$, or $\vec{F} = -\vec{\nabla}U$.

title: Loss of Kinetic Energy in 1D Collision
derivationOrExplanation: In center-of-mass frame, total kinetic energy before collision is $K_{initial} = \frac{1}{2}\mu (u_1 - u_2)^2$. Relative velocity after collision is $v_{rel} = e(u_1 - u_2)$, so final kinetic energy in CM frame is $K_{final} = \frac{1}{2}\mu [e(u_1 - u_2)]^2 = \frac{1}{2}\mu e^2 (u_1 - u_2)^2$. The difference is $\Delta K_{loss} = K_{initial} - K_{final} = \frac{1}{2}\mu (1 - e^2)(u_1 - u_2)^2$.

title: Bouncing Ball Height and Total Traveled Distance
formulaOrRule: h_n = e^{2n} h_0, \quad H_{total} = h_0 \left(\frac{1 + e^2}{1 - e^2}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Speed just before first impact is $v_0 = \sqrt{2gh_0}$. Speed right after first bounce is $v_1 = e v_0 = e\sqrt{2gh_0}$. Height reached is $h_1 = \frac{v_1^2}{2g} = e^2 h_0$. title: Combination of Springs
formulaOrRule: k_{eff} = k_1 + k_2 \quad (\text{Parallel}), \quad \frac{1}{k_{eff}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2} \quad (\text{Series})

title: Work Done by Kinetic Friction and Thermal Dissipation
formulaOrRule: W_{friction} = -f_k \cdot s_{rel}
derivationOrExplanation: Let surface 1 move by $s_1$ and surface 2 move by $s_2$. Work on 1 is $-f_k s_1$; work on 2 is $+f_k s_2$. Net mechanical work is $W_{net} = -f_k(s_1 - s_2) = -f_k s_{rel}$. This negative work precisely matches heat generated at the contact interface.

title: de Broglie Wavelength of Matter Waves
formulaOrRule: \lambda_{dB} = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}} \approx \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}} \text{ nm (for electron)}
derivationOrExplanation: Louis de Broglie hypothesized nature is symmetric: if photons have momentum $p = E/c = h\nu/c = h/\lambda$, matter particles must carry wavelength $\lambda = h/p$. For non-relativistic particle accelerated through voltage $V$: $K = qV = \frac{p^2}{2m} \implies p = \sqrt{2mqV}$. Hence $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$. For electron ($m = 9.109 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}, q = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$), this evaluates to $\lambda = \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ nm}$.

title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
formulaOrRule: \Delta x \cdot \Delta p_x \ge \frac{\hbar}{2} = \frac{h}{4\pi}, \quad \Delta E \cdot \Delta t \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}
derivationOrExplanation: Follows from Fourier transform properties of wavepackets: spatial width $\Delta x$ and wavenumber spread $\Delta k$ obey $\Delta x \Delta k \ge 1/2$. Using de Broglie relation $p = \hbar k \implies \Delta p = \hbar \Delta k$, multiplying by $\hbar$ yields $\Delta x \Delta p_x \ge \hbar / 2$.

title: Bohr Atomic Model: Orbital Radii
formulaOrRule: r_n = \frac{n^2 h^2 \epsilon_0}{\pi m e^2 Z} = \frac{n^2}{Z} a_0, \quad a_0 \approx 0.529 \text{ \AA}
derivationOrExplanation: Bohr's quantization postulate: $m v r = \frac{n h}{2\pi} \implies v = \frac{n h}{2\pi m r}$. Coulomb force supplies centripetal force: $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r^2} = \frac{m v^2}{r} = \frac{m}{r}\left(\frac{n h}{2\pi m r}\right)^2 = \frac{n^2 h^2}{4\pi^2 m r^3}$. Solving for $r$: $r_n = \frac{\epsilon_0 n^2 h^2}{\pi m Z e^2} = \frac{n^2}{Z} a_0$.

title: Bohr Atomic Model: Quantized Energy Levels
formulaOrRule: E_n = -\frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8 \epsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}
derivationOrExplanation: Kinetic energy: $K = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 = \frac{1}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r}$. Potential energy: $U = -\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r}$. Total energy: $E = K + U = -\frac{1}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Z e^2}{r} = -K = \frac{1}{2}U$. Substituting orbital radius $r_n$: $E_n = -\frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2}\text{ eV}$.

title: Rydberg Formula for Hydrogen Spectral Series
formulaOrRule: \frac{1}{\lambda} = R_H Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right), \quad R_H = 1.09737 \times 10^7 \text{ m}^{-1}

variablesOrTerms.n_1, n_2: Lower and higher energy quantum numbers ($n_2 > n_1$)

derivationOrExplanation: Conservation of energy: $E_{photon} = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1} = \frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^2}\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$. Dividing by $hc$: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = \left(\frac{m e^4}{8\epsilon_0^2 h^3 c}\right) Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right) = R_H Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$.

title: Law of Radioactive Decay
formulaOrRule: N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t} = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t / T_{1/2}}, \quad T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \approx \frac{0.693}{\lambda}, \quad \tau = \frac{1}{\lambda}
derivationOrExplanation: Rate of disintegration is directly proportional to present population: $-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N \implies \frac{dN}{N} = -\lambda dt$. Integrating from $t=0$ ($N=N_0$) to $t$: $\ln(N/N_0) = -\lambda t \implies N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$. At half-life $t = T_{1/2}$, $N = N_0 / 2$: $e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} = 1/2 \implies \lambda T_{1/2} = \ln 2 \implies T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \approx \frac{0.693}{\lambda}$. Mean life is $\tau = \frac{1}{N_0}\int_0^\infty N(t)dt = \frac{1}{\lambda}$.

title: Nuclear Mass Defect and Binding Energy
formulaOrRule: \Delta m = [Z m_p + (A - Z)m_n] - M_{nucleus}, \quad E_b = \Delta m \cdot c^2 = \Delta m (931.5 \text{ MeV/u})
derivationOrExplanation: Free nucleons have greater combined rest mass than the bound composite nucleus. The missing mass $\Delta m = Z m_p + (A-Z)m_n - M$ was liberated as binding energy during nucleosynthesis following Einstein's mass-energy equivalence $E = \Delta m \cdot c^2$. Using $1\text{ u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$ yields $1\text{ u} \equiv 931.5\text{ MeV}$.

title: Nuclear Radius and Constant Nuclear Density
formulaOrRule: R = R_0 A^{1/3}, \quad R_0 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m} = 1.2 \text{ fm}, \quad \rho_{nuclear} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17} \text{ kg/m}^3
derivationOrExplanation: High-energy electron scattering experiments demonstrate nuclear volume is directly proportional to number of nucleons $A$: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \propto A \implies R = R_0 A^{1/3}$. Nuclear mass is $M \approx A m_N$. Density is $\rho = \frac{M}{V} = \frac{A m_N}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \frac{3 m_N}{4\pi R_0^3} = \text{constant} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg/m}^3$.

title: Semiconductor Mass Action Law and Shockley Diode Equation
formulaOrRule: n_i^2 = n_e n_h \quad (\text{Mass Action Law}), \quad I = I_0 (e^{e V / \eta k_B T} - 1) \quad (\text{Diode Equation})
derivationOrExplanation: Law of Mass Action: thermal generation rate of electron-hole pairs equals recombination rate $R = r n_e n_h$. In thermal equilibrium, generation equals recombination, yielding $n_e n_h = n_i^2$, valid for both intrinsic and doped extrinsic semiconductors. Shockley diode equation follows from Boltzmann diffusion of majority carriers across depletion barrier: $I = I_0(e^{eV / \eta k_B T} - 1)$.

formulaOrRule: V_{ripple} = \frac{I_{dc}}{2 f C} \quad (\text{Full-Wave Rectifier with Capacitor Filter})

title: Duane-Hunt Law for Continuous X-Ray Cutoff
formulaOrRule: \lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{e V_a} = \frac{1240}{V_a} \text{ nm (Duane-Hunt Law)}
derivationOrExplanation: Electrons strike heavy metal target (Tungsten/Molybdenum) after gaining kinetic energy $K = e V_a$. title: Moseley's Law
formulaOrRule: \sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b) \quad (\text{Moseley's Law for Characteristic X-Rays})
derivationOrExplanation: Henry Moseley (1913) analyzed characteristic X-ray transitions: an inner $K$-shell vacancy is screened by remaining electron, so effective nuclear charge seen by transition electron is $Z_{eff} = Z - 1$. Applying Bohr formula: $\nu = R_H c (Z - 1)^2 \left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2}\right) = \frac{3}{4}R_H c (Z - 1)^2$. Taking square root: $\sqrt{\nu} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}R_H c}(Z - 1) = a(Z - 1)$.

title: Mirror Formula and Linear Magnification
formulaOrRule: \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}, \quad m = -\frac{v}{u} = \frac{f}{f - u}
derivationOrExplanation: From paraxial ray geometry of reflection on spherical mirror: similar triangles formed by object, image, and center of curvature give $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{v - R}{R - u} = -\frac{v}{u}$. Equating ratios and using $R = 2f$: $\frac{v - 2f}{2f - u} = \frac{v}{u} \implies u(v - 2f) = v(2f - u) \implies uv - 2uf = 2vf - uv \implies 2uv = 2f(u + v)$. Dividing both sides by $2uvf$ gives $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$.

title: Snell's Law of Refraction and Total Internal Reflection (TIR)
formulaOrRule: n_1 \sin\theta_1 = n_2 \sin\theta_2, \quad \sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \quad (n_1 > n_2)
derivationOrExplanation: From Fermat's Principle of Least Time: travel time between points $A(0, a)$ and $B(d, -b)$ across boundary at $(x, 0)$ is $t(x) = \frac{\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}}{v_1} + \frac{\sqrt{b^2 + (d-x)^2}}{v_2}$. Setting $\frac{dt}{dx} = 0$: $\frac{x}{v_1\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}} - \frac{d-x}{v_2\sqrt{b^2 + (d-x)^2}} = 0 \implies \frac{\sin\theta_1}{v_1} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{v_2}$. Multiplying by $c$ gives $n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$. At critical angle $\theta_c$, angle of refraction reaches $\theta_2 = 90^\circ \implies \sin\theta_c = n_2/n_1$.

title: Refraction at a Single Spherical Curved Surface
formulaOrRule: \frac{\mu_2}{v} - \frac{\mu_1}{u} = \frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}
derivationOrExplanation: From paraxial ray geometry: for small incident ray angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ with principal axis: $i = \alpha + \gamma$ and $\gamma = r + \beta \implies r = \gamma - \beta$. Snell's law in paraxial approximation is $\mu_1 i = \mu_2 r$. Substituting gives $\mu_1(\alpha + \gamma) = \mu_2(\gamma - \beta) \implies \mu_1 \alpha + \mu_2 \beta = (\mu_2 - \mu_1)\gamma$. For small angles, $\alpha \approx \frac{h}{-u}$, $\beta \approx \frac{h}{v}$, and $\gamma \approx \frac{h}{R}$. Canceling arc height $h$ yields $\frac{\mu_2}{v} - \frac{\mu_1}{u} = \frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$.

title: Lens Maker's Formula and Thin Lens Equation
formulaOrRule: \frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right), \quad \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}

variablesOrTerms.R_1, R_2: Radii of curvature of first and second faces

derivationOrExplanation: Apply spherical refraction formula to first surface of curvature $R_1$: $\frac{\mu}{v_1} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{\mu - 1}{R_1}$. For second surface of curvature $R_2$, $v_1$ acts as virtual object: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{\mu}{v_1} = \frac{1 - \mu}{R_2} = -\frac{\mu - 1}{R_2}$. Adding both equations eliminates intermediate image $v_1$: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$. For object at infinity ($u = \infty$), image forms at focus ($v = f$), giving $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$.

title: Optical Power and Combination of Lenses
formulaOrRule: P = \frac{1}{f} \text{ (Diopters)}, \quad P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2 - d P_1 P_2
derivationOrExplanation: Optical power measures deviation angle $\delta = h / f$ produced for a ray at unit height $h=1$, hence $P = 1/f$. For two lenses in close contact ($d=0$), net focal length is $\frac{1}{F} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} \implies P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2$. When separated by distance $d$, tracing ray deviation shows second lens receives incident ray at reduced height $h_2 = h_1 - d \delta_1 = h_1(1 - d/f_1)$, resulting in $P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2 - d P_1 P_2$.

title: Prism Formula at Minimum Deviation
formulaOrRule: \mu = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin(A / 2)}
derivationOrExplanation: Total deviation angle is $\delta = (i_1 + i_2) - A$ where $r_1 + r_2 = A$. title: Astronomical Refracting Telescope Magnification
formulaOrRule: M_{telescope} = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}, \quad L_{normal} = f_o + f_e, \quad M_{max} = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \frac{f_e}{D}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Objective forms intermediate inverted real image of distant object at its focal plane ($h' = f_o \alpha$). Eyepiece acts as simple magnifier: in normal adjustment (image at infinity), visual angle is $\beta = h'/f_e$. Angular magnification is $M = \frac{\beta}{\alpha} = \frac{h'/f_e}{h'/f_o} = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}$. Separation between lenses is tube length $L = f_o + f_e$. If image forms at near point $D$, eyepiece magnification is $m_e = 1 + D/f_e$, yielding $M = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \frac{f_e}{D}\right)$.

title: Compound Microscope Magnification
formulaOrRule: M_{microscope} = -\frac{v_o}{u_o}\left(\frac{D}{f_e}\right) \approx -\frac{L}{f_o}\left(\frac{D}{f_e}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Total magnification is product of linear magnification of objective $m_o = -v_o / u_o$ and angular magnification of eyepiece $m_e = D / f_e$ (at infinity): $M = m_o \times m_e = -\left(\frac{v_o}{u_o}\right)\left(\frac{D}{f_e}\right)$. In standard microscope geometry, object is placed just outside $f_o$ ($u_o \approx f_o$) and image forms near eyepiece ($v_o \approx L$), giving $M \approx -\frac{L D}{f_o f_e}$.

title: Young's Double Slit Experiment (YDSE) Fringe Width and Intensity
formulaOrRule: \beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}, \quad I(\Delta\phi) = 4 I_0 \cos^2\left(\frac{\Delta\phi}{2}\right), \quad \Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\left(\frac{y d}{D}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Path difference between rays from two slits is $\Delta x = d\sin\theta \approx d\frac{y}{D}$. Bright fringes occur at constructive interference: $\Delta x = n\lambda \implies y_n = n\frac{\lambda D}{d}$. Spacing between consecutive fringes is fringe width $\beta = y_{n+1} - y_n = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$. Phase difference is $\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x = \frac{2\pi y d}{\lambda D}$. Superposing two coherent waves $E = E_0 e^{i\omega t} + E_0 e^{i(\omega t + \Delta\phi)}$ gives resultant amplitude $E_R = 2E_0\cos(\Delta\phi/2)$, so intensity is $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\Delta\phi/2)$.

title: Fringe Shift in YDSE Due to Thin Transparent Plate
formulaOrRule: \Delta y = \frac{(\mu - 1)t D}{d}
derivationOrExplanation: Optical path length through sheet of thickness $t$ is $\mu t$ instead of geometric air path $t$. Extra optical path introduced in that beam is $\Delta_{opt} = \mu t - t = (\mu - 1)t$. Central fringe now occurs where net path difference vanishes: $d\frac{y_0}{D} - (\mu - 1)t = 0 \implies y_0 = \frac{(\mu - 1)t D}{d}$. Number of shifted fringes is $N = \frac{\Delta y}{\beta} = \frac{(\mu - 1)t}{\lambda}$.

title: Single-Slit Fraunhofer Diffraction
formulaOrRule: a \sin\theta = m\lambda \quad (\text{Minima}), \quad y_1 = \frac{\lambda D}{a}, \quad W_{central} = \frac{2\lambda D}{a}

variablesOrTerms.W_{central}: Linear width of central maximum on screen

derivationOrExplanation: Divide slit of width $a$ into two equal halves of width $a/2$: path difference between corresponding wavelets from top and middle is $\frac{a}{2}\sin\theta$. Destructive interference occurs when this path difference is $\lambda/2 \implies \frac{a}{2}\sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{2} \implies a\sin\theta = \lambda$. In general, dividing into $2m$ zones gives dark minima at $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$. Central maximum extends between first minima on either side ($m = \pm 1$): angular half-width $\theta_1 = \lambda/a$, so linear full width is $W_{central} = 2y_1 = 2\frac{\lambda D}{a}$.

title: Rayleigh's Criterion for Resolving Power
formulaOrRule: \theta_R = 1.22 \frac{\lambda}{D_{aperture}}, \quad \text{RP}_{telescope} = \frac{D_{aperture}}{1.22\lambda}
derivationOrExplanation: Diffraction of plane wave by circular aperture produces Airy disc pattern with first dark ring at angular radius $\theta = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}$ (derived from zeros of first-order Bessel function $J_1(x) = 0$). Lord Rayleigh postulated that two sources are barely resolved when the central maximum of one Airy disc falls exactly on the first minimum of the other: $\theta_R = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}$.

title: Polarization: Malus's Law and Brewster's Angle
formulaOrRule: I(\theta) = I_0 \cos^2\theta \quad (\text{Malus's Law}), \quad \tan\theta_p = \mu \quad (\text{Brewster's Law})
derivationOrExplanation: Malus's Law: electric field vector $\vec{E}_0$ of polarized wave incident at angle $\theta$ to transmission axis has transmitted component $E = E_0\cos\theta$. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared: $I(\theta) \propto E^2 = E_0^2\cos^2\theta = I_0\cos^2\theta$. Brewster's Law: reflected ray is completely polarized perpendicular to plane of incidence when reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular ($r + \theta_p = 90^\circ \implies r = 90^\circ - \theta_p$). Substituting into Snell's law: $\sin\theta_p = \mu \sin r = \mu \sin(90^\circ - \theta_p) = \mu \cos\theta_p \implies \tan\theta_p = \mu$.

title: Fundamental Adjoint Theorem for Square Matrix
formulaOrRule: A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = \text{adj}(A) \cdot A = |A| I_n
derivationOrExplanation: Entry $(i, j)$ of $A \cdot \text{adj}(A)$ is $\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} [\text{adj}(A)]_{kj} = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik} C_{jk}$ where $C_{jk}$ is cofactor. By Laplace expansion: If $i = j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{ik} = |A|$. If $i \ne j$, $\sum A_{ik} C_{jk} = 0$ (expansion of determinant with two identical rows). Thus $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$.

title: Matrix Inversion Formula
formulaOrRule: A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A) \quad (|A| \ne 0)

variablesOrTerms.A^{-1}: multiplicative inverse satisfying A * A^{-1} = I

derivationOrExplanation: From $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$. For non-singular matrix $|A| \ne 0$, divide both sides by scalar $|A|$: $A \cdot \left(\frac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)\right) = I_n$. By uniqueness of matrix inverse: $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)$.

title: Determinant of Adjoint Matrix
formulaOrRule: |\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^{n - 1}
derivationOrExplanation: Take determinant of both sides of $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) = |A| I_n$: $|A \cdot \text{adj}(A)| = ||A| I_n|$. Using properties $|XY| = |X||Y|$ and $|k I_n| = k^n$: $|A| \cdot |\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^n$. For $|A| \ne 0$, divide by $|A|$: $|\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^{n-1}$. Holds by continuity for $|A| = 0$ as well.

title: Double Adjoint Matrix Identities
formulaOrRule: |\text{adj}(\text{adj}(A))| = |A|^{(n - 1)^2}, \quad \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |A|^{n - 2} A
derivationOrExplanation: Replace $A$ with $B = \text{adj}(A)$ in adjoint formula: $B \cdot \text{adj}(B) = |B| I \implies \text{adj}(A) \cdot \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |\text{adj}(A)| I = |A|^{n-1} I$. Multiply on left by $A$: $A \cdot \text{adj}(A) \cdot \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = A |A|^{n-1} I \implies |A| I \cdot \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |A|^{n-1} A \implies \text{adj}(\text{adj}(A)) = |A|^{n-2} A$. Taking determinant gives $|A|^{(n-1)^2}$.

title: Reversal Law for Inverses and Transposes
derivationOrExplanation: For transpose: $[(AB)^T]_{ij} = [AB]_{ji} = \sum A_{jk} B_{ki} = \sum B^T_{ik} A^T_{kj} = [B^T A^T]_{ij}$. For inverse: $(AB)(B^{-1} A^{-1}) = A(B B^{-1})A^{-1} = A I A^{-1} = A A^{-1} = I$. Thus by inverse uniqueness $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}$.

flashcard.front: What is Reversal Law for Inverses and Transposes?
flashcard.back:
(A B)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}, \quad (A B)^T = B^T A^T
For transpose: $[(AB)^T]_{ij} = [AB]_{ji} = \sum A_{jk} B_{ki} = \sum B^T_{ik} A^T_{kj} = [B^T A^T]_{ij}$. For inverse: $(AB)(B^{-1} A^{-1}) = A(B B^{-1})A^{-1} = A I A^{-1} = A A^{-1} = I$. Thus by inverse uniqueness $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}$.

title: Unique Decomposition into Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices
formulaOrRule: A = \frac{1}{2}(A + A^T) + \frac{1}{2}(A - A^T) \implies \text{Symmetric} + \text{Skew-Symmetric}
derivationOrExplanation: Direct algebra: $\frac{1}{2}(A + A^T) + \frac{1}{2}(A - A^T) = \frac{1}{2}A + \frac{1}{2}A^T + \frac{1}{2}A - \frac{1}{2}A^T = A$. Test symmetry of $P$: $P^T = [\frac{1}{2}(A+A^T)]^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T+A) = P$. Test skew-symmetry of $Q$: $Q^T = [\frac{1}{2}(A-A^T)]^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T-A) = -Q$. Diagonal elements of $Q$ must be zero.

title: Cramer's Rule for System of 3 Linear Equations
formulaOrRule: x = \frac{\Delta_x}{\Delta}, \quad y = \frac{\Delta_y}{\Delta}, \quad z = \frac{\Delta_z}{\Delta} \quad (\Delta \ne 0)

title: Consistency Criteria for Non-Homogeneous Linear Systems

title: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
formulaOrRule: p(A) = 0 \quad \text{where } p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I) = 0
derivationOrExplanation: From matrix identity $(A - \lambda I) \cdot \text{adj}(A - \lambda I) = \det(A - \lambda I) I = p(\lambda) I$. The matrix $\text{adj}(A - \lambda I)$ is a polynomial in $\lambda$ of degree $n-1$: $B_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1} + \dots + B_1 \lambda + B_0$. Equating powers of $\lambda$ and summing matrix products eliminates intermediate matrices $B_k$, proving $p(A) = A^n + c_{n-1} A^{n-1} + \dots + c_0 I = 0$.

title: Orthogonal Matrix Definition and Properties
formulaOrRule: A A^T = A^T A = I \implies A^{-1} = A^T, \quad |A| = \pm 1
derivationOrExplanation: By definition $A A^T = I$. Taking determinants: $|A A^T| = |I| \implies |A| |A^T| = 1$. Since $|A^T| = |A|$: $|A|^2 = 1 \implies |A| = \pm 1$. Multiplying $A A^T = I$ by $A^{-1}$ from left: $A^T = A^{-1}$. Columns and rows of orthogonal matrix form an orthonormal basis ($\vec{v}_i \cdot \vec{v}_j = \delta_{ij}$).

title: Scalar Multiplication Property of Determinants
formulaOrRule: |k A| = k^n |A| \quad \text{for } n \times n \text{ matrix}
derivationOrExplanation: Multiplying matrix $A$ by scalar $k$ multiplies every entry in every row by $k$. Determinant property: factoring $k$ out of a single row scales determinant by $k$. Since there are $n$ rows in an $n \times n$ matrix, factoring $k$ out of all $n$ rows gives $k \times k \times \dots \times k = k^n$. Thus $|kA| = k^n |A|$.

title: Vandermonde Determinant Identity
formulaOrRule: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix} = (a - b)(b - c)(c - a)
derivationOrExplanation: Perform row operations $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \rightarrow R_3 - R_1$: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 0 & b-a & b^2-a^2 \\ 0 & c-a & c^2-a^2 \end{vmatrix}$. Factor $(b-a)$ from row 2 and $(c-a)$ from row 3: $(b-a)(c-a) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 0 & 1 & b+a \\ 0 & 1 & c+a \end{vmatrix}$. Expanding along first column: $(b-a)(c-a)[(c+a) - (b+a)] = (b-a)(c-a)(c-b) = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$.

title: Euler Form and Polar Representation
formulaOrRule: z = x + i y = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r e^{i\theta}

Multiplying by modulus $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ gives $z = r e^{i\theta}$.

title: Cube Roots of Unity Fundamental Identities
formulaOrRule: 1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0, \quad \omega^3 = 1 \quad \left(\omega = e^{i 2\pi/3} = -\frac{1}{2} + i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Solve $z^3 - 1 = 0 \implies (z-1)(z^2+z+1) = 0$. Non-real roots satisfy $z^2+z+1=0$. Let $\omega = \frac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2} = e^{i 2\pi/3}$. Then $\omega^2 = e^{i 4\pi/3} = \frac{-1-i\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Sum: $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 1 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}+i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) + \left(-\frac{1}{2}-i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 0$. Product: $\omega^3 = e^{i 2\pi} = 1$.

title: n-th Roots of Unity and Geometric Properties
formulaOrRule: z_k = e^{i \frac{2k\pi}{n}}, \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1 \implies \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} z_k = 0, \quad \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} z_k = (-1)^{n-1}
derivationOrExplanation: Roots of $z^n - 1 = 0$ are vertices of regular $n$-gon on unit circle: $z_k = \omega_n^k$ where $\omega_n = e^{i 2\pi/n}$. Sum is sum of finite GP: $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \omega_n^k = \frac{1 - \omega_n^n}{1 - \omega_n} = \frac{1 - 1}{1 - \omega_n} = 0$. Product from constant term in $z^n - 1 = \prod (z - z_k)$: $\prod z_k = (-1)^n (-1) = (-1)^{n-1}$.

title: Locus of Perpendicular Bisector
formulaOrRule: |z - z_1| = |z - z_2| \implies \text{Perpendicular bisector of segment joining } z_1 \text{ and } z_2

title: Angle in Semicircle Locus
formulaOrRule: \text{Arg}\left(\frac{z - z_1}{z - z_2}\right) = \pm \frac{\pi}{2} \implies \text{Circle with diameter } z_1 z_2
derivationOrExplanation: Angle subtended by segment $z_1-z_2$ at point $z$ is $\theta = \text{Arg}\left(\frac{z - z_1}{z - z_2}\right)$. title: Condition for Equilateral Triangle in Complex Plane
formulaOrRule: z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 = z_1 z_2 + z_2 z_3 + z_3 z_1 \implies \text{Equilateral Triangle}
derivationOrExplanation: In equilateral triangle, side $z_3 - z_1$ is obtained by rotating $z_2 - z_1$ by $60^\circ$ ($e^{i\pi/3} = -\omega^2$): $\frac{z_3 - z_1}{z_2 - z_1} = e^{i\pi/3} = 1 + \omega$. Similarly $\frac{z_1 - z_2}{z_3 - z_2} = e^{i\pi/3}$. Eliminating angles and simplifying: $(z_1 - z_2)^2 + (z_2 - z_3)^2 + (z_3 - z_1)^2 = 0 \implies 2(z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2) - 2(z_1 z_2 + z_2 z_3 + z_3 z_1) = 0 \implies z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 = z_1 z_2 + z_2 z_3 + z_3 z_1$.

title: Conjugate Fundamental Identities
formulaOrRule: \text{Re}(z) = \frac{z + \bar{z}}{2}, \quad \text{Im}(z) = \frac{z - \bar{z}}{2i}, \quad z \bar{z} = |z|^2

formulaOrRule: \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \cos\theta = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3

formulaOrRule: [\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}

variablesOrTerms.V = |[\\vec{a} \\vec{b} \\vec{c}]|: volume of parallelepiped spanned by vectors a, b, c

derivationOrExplanation: Volume of parallelepiped = $(\text{Base Area}) \times (\text{Height})$. Base is parallelogram spanned by $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$, so area vector is $\vec{A} = \vec{b} \times \vec{c}$. Height is projection of $\vec{a}$ onto normal $\hat{n} = \frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|}$: $h = |\vec{a}||\cos\phi|$. Volume $= |\vec{b}\times\vec{c}| |\vec{a}| |\cos\phi| = |\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b}\times\vec{c})|$. Substituting determinant components for cross and dot products yields the $3 \times 3$ determinant.

title: Vector Triple Product (BAC-CAB Rule)
formulaOrRule: \vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}) \vec{b} - (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) \vec{c} \quad (\text{BAC - CAB Rule})
derivationOrExplanation: The vector $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$, so it lies in the plane of $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$: $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = x \vec{b} + y \vec{c}$. It is also perpendicular to $\vec{a}$, so $\vec{a} \cdot [x\vec{b} + y\vec{c}] = 0 \implies x(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}) + y(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}) = 0 \implies \frac{x}{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}} = -\frac{y}{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}} = \lambda$. Evaluating with standard basis vectors (e.g. $\vec{a}=\hat{i}, \vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}, \vec{c}=\hat{k}$) determines $\lambda = 1$. Thus $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b} - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}$.

title: Lagrange's Vector Identity
formulaOrRule: |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 - (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})^2
derivationOrExplanation: By definition: $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 = (|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta)^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 \sin^2\theta$. Use Pythagorean trigonometric identity $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta$: $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 (1 - \cos^2\theta) = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 - (|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta)^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2$.

title: Direction Cosines of a Line in 3D Space
formulaOrRule: l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1, \quad \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1, \quad \sin^2\alpha + \sin^2\beta + \sin^2\gamma = 2

variablesOrTerms.\\alpha, \\beta, \\gamma: angles made by line with positive x, y, z coordinate axes

derivationOrExplanation: Let $\hat{u}$ be a unit vector along the line: $\hat{u} = l\hat{i} + m\hat{j} + n\hat{k}$. Since it is a unit vector: $|\hat{u}|^2 = l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$. Since $l = \cos\alpha, m = \cos\beta, n = \cos\gamma$: $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$. Using $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta$: $(1 - \sin^2\alpha) + (1 - \sin^2\beta) + (1 - \sin^2\gamma) = 1 \implies \sin^2\alpha + \sin^2\beta + \sin^2\gamma = 3 - 1 = 2$.

title: Symmetric Cartesian Equation of a Straight Line in 3D
formulaOrRule: \frac{x - x_1}{a} = \frac{y - y_1}{b} = \frac{z - z_1}{c} = \lambda
derivationOrExplanation: Let $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ be an arbitrary point on the line passing through point $A(\vec{a}) = x_1\hat{i} + y_1\hat{j} + z_1\hat{k}$ parallel to direction vector $\vec{b} = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$. Vector equation: $\vec{r} - \vec{a} = \lambda \vec{b} \implies (x - x_1)\hat{i} + (y - y_1)\hat{j} + (z - z_1)\hat{k} = \lambda(a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k})$. Equating components: $x - x_1 = \lambda a, y - y_1 = \lambda b, z - z_1 = \lambda c \implies \lambda = \frac{x - x_1}{a} = \frac{y - y_1}{b} = \frac{z - z_1}{c}$.

title: Shortest Distance Between Two Skew Lines
formulaOrRule: d = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}
derivationOrExplanation: The common perpendicular line segment connecting the two skew lines is parallel to $\vec{n} = \vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$. Unit normal is $\hat{n} = \frac{\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$. The shortest distance $d$ is the magnitude of the projection of the displacement vector $\vec{a}_2 - \\vec{a}_1$ joining points on the two lines onto this common normal: $d = |(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot \hat{n}| = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$.

title: Condition for Two Lines in 3D to be Coplanar
formulaOrRule: (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = 0 \iff \begin{vmatrix} x_2 - x_1 & y_2 - y_1 & z_2 - z_1 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{vmatrix} = 0
derivationOrExplanation: Two lines are coplanar if and only if the shortest distance between them is zero. From the shortest distance formula, numerator vanishing gives $(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = 0$. Writing displacement $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1$ and direction vectors $\vec{b}_1, \vec{b}_2$ in determinant form yields the coplanarity determinant equation.

title: General Equation of a Plane in 3D Space
formulaOrRule: A x + B y + C z + D = 0 \iff \vec{r} \cdot \vec{n} = d
derivationOrExplanation: Let plane pass through point $P_0(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with normal vector $\vec{n} = A\hat{i} + B\hat{j} + C\hat{k}$. For any point $P(x, y, z)$ on the plane, the vector $\vec{P_0 P} = (x-x_0)\hat{i} + (y-y_0)\hat{j} + (z-z_0)\hat{k}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{n}$: $\vec{P_0 P} \cdot \vec{n} = 0 \implies A(x - x_0) + B(y - y_0) + C(z - z_0) = 0 \implies Ax + By + Cz - (Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0) = 0$. Setting constant $D = -(Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0)$ gives $Ax + By + Cz + D = 0$.

title: Perpendicular Distance from Point (x0, y0, z0) to Plane
formulaOrRule: d = \frac{|A x_0 + B y_0 + C z_0 + D|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}}
derivationOrExplanation: Line through $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ along normal $\vec{n}$ has equation $\vec{r}(t) = (x_0 + At)\hat{i} + (y_0 + Bt)\hat{j} + (z_0 + Ct)\hat{k}$. Substitute into plane equation: $A(x_0 + At) + B(y_0 + Bt) + C(z_0 + Ct) + D = 0 \implies (A x_0 + B y_0 + C z_0 + D) + t(A^2 + B^2 + C^2) = 0 \implies t = -\\frac{A x_0 + B y_0 + C z_0 + D}{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}$. The distance is the displacement magnitude: $d = |t| |\vec{n}| = \\frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0 + D|}{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} \\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} = \\frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0 + D|}{\\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}}$.

formulaOrRule: \sin\phi = \frac{|A a + B b + C c|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}} = \frac{|\vec{n} \cdot \vec{b}|}{|\vec{n}| |\vec{b}|}

The angle $\phi$ that the line makes with the plane is complementary to $\theta$: $\phi = 90^\circ - \theta$. title: Family of Planes Passing Through Line of Intersection
formulaOrRule: P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0 \iff (A_1 x + B_1 y + C_1 z + D_1) + \lambda (A_2 x + B_2 y + C_2 z + D_2) = 0

variablesOrTerms.\\lambda: real parameter determined by boundary condition

derivationOrExplanation: Let line of intersection of planes $P_1 = 0$ and $P_2 = 0$ be $L$. For any point $(x, y, z)$ on line $L$, both $P_1(x, y, z) = 0$ and $P_2(x, y, z) = 0$ are satisfied simultaneously. Thus $P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0 + \lambda(0) = 0$ for any value of $\lambda$. Furthermore, $P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0$ is linear in $x, y, z$, so it represents a plane. Hence it represents every plane passing through the intersection line $L$.

title: Compound Angle Addition and Subtraction Formulas
formulaOrRule: \sin(A \pm B) = \sin A \cos B \pm \cos A \sin B, \quad \cos(A \pm B) = \cos A \cos B \mp \sin A \sin B
derivationOrExplanation: In the unit circle, consider unit vectors $\vec{u} = \cos A \hat{i} + \sin A \hat{j}$ and $\vec{v} = \cos B \hat{i} + \sin B \hat{j}$. The angle between them is $A - B$. Scalar dot product: $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = (1)(1)\cos(A - B)$. Component dot product: $\cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Equating gives $\cos(A - B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$. Replacing $B$ with $-B$ yields $\cos(A + B)$. Using co-function identities $\sin\theta = \cos(\pi/2 - \theta)$ gives the sine compound formulas.

title: Tangent of Compound Angles
formulaOrRule: \tan(A \pm B) = \frac{\tan A \pm \tan B}{1 \mp \tan A \tan B}
derivationOrExplanation: By definition: $\tan(A + B) = \frac{\sin(A + B)}{\cos(A + B)} = \frac{\sin A \cos B + \cos A \sin B}{\cos A \cos B - \sin A \sin B}$. Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos A \cos B$: $\tan(A + B) = \frac{\frac{\sin A \cos B}{\cos A \cos B} + \frac{\cos A \sin B}{\cos A \cos B}}{\frac{\cos A \cos B}{\cos A \cos B} - \frac{\sin A \sin B}{\cos A \cos B}} = \frac{\tan A + \\tan B}{1 - \\tan A \\tan B}$. Replacing $B$ with $-B$ and using $\tan(-B) = -\tan B$ yields the subtraction formula.

title: Sum-to-Product Trigonometric Identities
formulaOrRule: \sin C + \sin D = 2 \sin\left(\frac{C + D}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{C - D}{2}\right), \quad \cos C + \cos D = 2 \cos\left(\frac{C + D}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{C - D}{2}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Let $A = \frac{C + D}{2}$ and $B = \frac{C - D}{2}$, so $A + B = C$ and $A - B = D$. Using compound angle identities: $\sin(A + B) = \sin A \cos B + \cos A \sin B$ and $\sin(A - B) = \sin A \cos B - \cos A \sin B$. Adding both equations: $\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B) = 2 \sin A \cos B \implies \sin C + \sin D = 2 \sin\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right)$. Similarly, adding cosine compound identities yields $\cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{C-D}{2}\right)$.

formulaOrRule: \sin(2A) = 2 \sin A \cos A = \frac{2 \tan A}{1 + \tan^2 A}, \quad \cos(2A) = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = 2\cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 A = \frac{1 - \tan^2 A}{1 + \tan^2 A}

For cosine: $\cos(2A) = \cos(A + A) = \cos A \cos A - \sin A \sin A = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A$. Using $\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1$ yields $2\cos^2 A - 1$ and $1 - 2\sin^2 A$.

formulaOrRule: \tan(2A) = \frac{2 \tan A}{1 - \tan^2 A}, \quad \sin(3A) = 3\sin A - 4\sin^3 A, \quad \cos(3A) = 4\cos^3 A - 3\cos A

formulaOrRule: \cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2 b c}, \quad a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2 b c \cos A
derivationOrExplanation: Place vertex $A$ at origin $(0, 0)$ with side $c$ along positive x-axis so $B = (c, 0)$. Vertex $C$ has coordinates $(b\cos A, b\sin A)$. title: Triangle Area and Heron's Formula
formulaOrRule: \Delta = \frac{1}{2} a b \sin C = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)} \quad \left(s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Area is $\frac{1}{2}(\text{base})(\text{height}) = \frac{1}{2}a(b\sin C) = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$. To derive Heron's formula: $\sin^2 C = 1 - \cos^2 C = (1 - \cos C)(1 + \cos C)$. Substitute cosine rule $\cos C = \frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}$: $1 - \cos C = \frac{c^2 - (a-b)^2}{2ab} = \frac{(c - a + b)(c + a - b)}{2ab} = \frac{2(s-a)2(s-b)}{2ab}$. Similarly $1 + \cos C = \frac{2s 2(s-c)}{2ab}$. Multiplying: $\sin^2 C = \frac{16 s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}{4a^2 b^2}$. Thus $\Delta = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$.

title: Addition Formula for Inverse Tangent
formulaOrRule: \tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1} y = \begin{cases} \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x + y}{1 - x y}\right) & \text{if } x y < 1 \\ \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x + y}{1 - x y}\right) & \text{if } x > 0, y > 0, x y > 1 \\ -\pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x + y}{1 - x y}\right) & \text{if } x < 0, y < 0, x y > 1 \end{cases}
derivationOrExplanation: Let $\alpha = \tan^{-1} x$ and $\beta = \tan^{-1} y \implies \tan\alpha = x, \tan\beta = y$ with $\alpha, \beta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$. Using compound angle: $\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta} = \frac{x + y}{1 - xy}$. If $xy < 1$, then $\alpha + \beta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$ lies inside the principal range of $\tan^{-1}$, so $\alpha + \beta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\right)$. If $x, y > 0$ and $xy > 1$, $\alpha + \beta \in (\pi/2, \pi)$, requiring subtraction of $\pi$: $\alpha + \beta = \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\right)$.

title: Complementary Angles Property of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
formulaOrRule: \sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \quad \tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \quad \sec^{-1} x + \csc^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}
derivationOrExplanation: Let $\theta = \sin^{-1} x \implies x = \sin\theta$. Using co-function identity: $x = \cos(\pi/2 - \theta)$. Taking principal $\cos^{-1}$ on both sides (since $\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2] \implies \pi/2 - \theta \in [0, \pi]$, which is the principal branch of $\cos^{-1}$): $\cos^{-1} x = \pi/2 - \theta = \pi/2 - \sin^{-1} x \implies \sin^{-1} x + \\cos^{-1} x = \\pi/2$. Same logic applies to $\tan^{-1}$ and $\cot^{-1}$.

title: Standard Trigonometric Limits
formulaOrRule: \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1, \quad \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan x}{x} = 1
derivationOrExplanation: In unit circle, for $0 < x < \pi/2$: area of sector $OAP$ is $\frac{1}{2}(1)^2 x = x/2$. Area of inscribed $\Delta OAP$ is $\frac{1}{2}(1)(\sin x) = \frac{\sin x}{2}$. Area of circumscribed triangle $OAT$ is $\frac{1}{2}(1)(\tan x) = \frac{\tan x}{2}$. Thus $\frac{\sin x}{2} < \frac{x}{2} < \frac{\tan x}{2} \implies \sin x < x < \tan x$. Divide by $\sin x$: $1 < \frac{x}{\sin x} < \frac{1}{\cos x} \implies \cos x < \frac{\sin x}{x} < 1$. As $x \to 0$, $\cos x \to 1$. By Sandwich Theorem: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$.

title: L'Hôpital's Rule for Indeterminate Forms
formulaOrRule: \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} \quad \left(\text{for } \frac{0}{0} \text{ or } \frac{\pm\infty}{\pm\infty}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Apply Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem to $f$ and $g$ on $[c, x]$: There exists $\xi$ between $c$ and $x$ such that $\frac{f(x) - f(c)}{g(x) - g(c)} = \frac{f'(\xi)}{g'(\xi)}$. Since $f(c) = g(c) = 0$: $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{f'(\xi)}{g'(\xi)}$. As $x \to c$, $\xi \to c$ by the squeeze theorem, giving $\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{\xi \to c} \frac{f'(\xi)}{g'(\xi)} = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$.

formulaOrRule: \frac{d}{dx}[u v] = u' v + u v', \quad \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{u}{v}\right] = \frac{u' v - u v'}{v^2}
derivationOrExplanation: For product: $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{u(x+h)v(x+h) - u(x)v(x)}{h} = \lim \frac{u(x+h)v(x+h) - u(x+h)v(x) + u(x+h)v(x) - u(x)v(x)}{h} = u(x)v'(x) + v(x)u'(x)$. title: Chain Rule for Composite Functions
formulaOrRule: \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx} \quad \text{for } y = f(u(x))
derivationOrExplanation: $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u} \cdot \frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}$ for $\Delta u \ne 0$. title: Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem (LMVT)
formulaOrRule: f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} \quad (c \in (a, b))

variablesOrTerms.f: continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b)

derivationOrExplanation: Construct secant line $L(x) = f(a) + \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(x - a)$. Define auxiliary function $h(x) = f(x) - L(x)$. Note $h(a) = f(a) - f(a) = 0$ and $h(b) = f(b) - f(b) = 0$. Since $h$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $h(a) = h(b) = 0$, Rolle's Theorem guarantees a point $c \in (a, b)$ where $h'(c) = 0$. $h'(c) = f'(c) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} = 0 \implies f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.

title: Equations of Tangent and Normal Lines to Curve y = f(x)
derivationOrExplanation: The slope of the tangent line to $y = f(x)$ at $(x_0, y_0)$ is the derivative $m_T = f'(x_0)$. By the point-slope formula of a straight line: $y - y_0 = m_T (x - x_0) = f'(x_0)(x - x_0)$. The normal line is perpendicular to the tangent line at the point of tangency, so its slope is $m_N = -1/m_T = -1/f'(x_0)$ (for $f'(x_0) \ne 0$). Hence normal equation: $y - y_0 = -\frac{1}{f'(x_0)}(x - x_0)$.

title: Angle of Intersection Between Two Curves
formulaOrRule: \tan\theta = \left|\frac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1 m_2}\right| = \left|\frac{f_1'(x_0) - f_2'(x_0)}{1 + f_1'(x_0) f_2'(x_0)}\right|

variablesOrTerms.m_1, m_2: tangent slopes of curves at intersection point (x0, y0)

derivationOrExplanation: The angle of intersection between two curves at a common point of intersection is defined as the angle between their tangent lines. Let the tangent lines make angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ with the positive x-axis so that $m_1 = \tan\theta_1$ and $m_2 = \tan\theta_2$. The angle between the lines is $\theta = |\theta_1 - \theta_2|$. Using compound angle identity: $\tan\theta = |\tan(\theta_1 - \theta_2)| = \left|\frac{\tan\theta_1 - \tan\theta_2}{1 + \tan\theta_1 \tan\theta_2}\right| = \left|\frac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1 m_2}\right|$. Curves are orthogonal if $m_1 m_2 = -1$.

title: AM-GM-HM Classical Means Inequality
formulaOrRule: \text{AM} \ge \text{GM} \ge \text{HM} \implies \frac{a_1 + \dots + a_n}{n} \ge \sqrt[n]{a_1 \dots a_n} \ge \frac{n}{\sum \frac{1}{a_i}}

title: Sum of First n Natural Numbers
formulaOrRule: \sum_{k=1}^n k = \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}
derivationOrExplanation: Using identity $(k+1)^2 - k^2 = 2k + 1$. Summing from $k=1$ to $n$: $\sum_{k=1}^n [(k+1)^2 - k^2] = 2\sum k + \sum 1 \implies (n+1)^2 - 1 = 2\sum k + n \implies n^2 + 2n = 2\sum k + n \implies 2\sum k = n^2 + n = n(n+1) \implies \sum k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

title: Molecular Orbital Bond Order
formulaOrRule: \text{Bond Order} = \frac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)

variablesOrTerms.N_a: Number of electrons in antibonding MOs
variablesOrTerms.N_b: Number of electrons in bonding MOs

derivationOrExplanation: Bonding molecular orbitals concentrate electron density between nuclei, lowering system potential energy and stabilizing molecule. Antibonding orbitals contain a nodal plane between nuclei, increasing nuclear repulsion and destabilizing molecule by an equal/greater amount. Each bonding pair contributes $+1$ net bond, while each antibonding pair cancels one bond: $\text{Bond Order} = \frac{N_b - N_a}{2}$.

title: Steric Number and Hybridization Formula
formulaOrRule: SN = \frac{1}{2}(V + M - C + A)

variablesOrTerms.M: Number of monovalent surrounding atoms (H, F, Cl, Br, I)

derivationOrExplanation: VSEPR postulates that valence electron pairs (bonding pairs and lone pairs) repel each other and position themselves as far apart as possible in 3D space to minimize electrostatic repulsion energy. Total electron domain count is $SN = \frac{V + M - C + A}{2}$. Hybridization state corresponds to: $SN=2 \implies sp$ (linear, $180^\circ$); $SN=3 \implies sp^2$ (trigonal planar, $120^\circ$); $SN=4 \implies sp^3$ (tetrahedral, $109.5^\circ$); $SN=5 \implies sp^3d$ (trigonal bipyramidal); $SN=6 \implies sp^3d^2$ (octahedral).

title: Born-Lande Equation for Lattice Energy
formulaOrRule: U_0 = -\frac{N_A M z_+ z_- e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r_0}\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Total potential energy per ion pair is sum of long-range Coulomb attractive terms and short-range Born repulsive core potentials: $U(r) = -\frac{M z_+ z_- e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} + \frac{B}{r^n}$. Setting derivative to zero at equilibrium separation $r_0$: $\left(\frac{dU}{dr}\right)_{r_0} = 0 \implies B = \frac{M z_+ z_- e^2 r_0^{n-1}}{4\pi\epsilon_0 n}$. Substituting $B$ back into energy expression yields $U_0 = -\frac{N_A M z_+ z_- e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r_0}\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)$.

title: Born-Haber Cycle for Ionic Solid Formation
formulaOrRule: \Delta H_f^\circ = \Delta H_{sub} + \frac{1}{2}\Delta H_{diss} + IE + EA + U_{lattice}

variablesOrTerms.\\Delta H_{diss}: Bond dissociation enthalpy of nonmetal gas

derivationOrExplanation: By Hess's Law of constant heat summation, enthalpy change between initial elements in standard states ($Na_{(s)} + \frac{1}{2}Cl_{2(g)}$) and crystalline product ($NaCl_{(s)}$) is independent of path. Indirect path vaporizes metal ($\Delta H_{sub}$), atomizes nonmetal ($\frac{1}{2}\Delta H_{diss}$), ionizes metal ($IE$), adds electron to nonmetal ($EA$), and condenses gas ions into solid lattice ($U_{lattice}$). Summing gives $\Delta H_f^\circ = \Delta H_{sub} + \frac{1}{2}\Delta H_{diss} + IE + EA + U_{lattice}$.

title: Fajans' Rules for Covalent Character in Ionic Bonds
formulaOrRule: \text{Polarizability } \alpha \propto \frac{\text{Anion Radius}^3}{\text{Cation Radius}^2} \quad (\text{Fajans' Rules})
derivationOrExplanation: Kasimir Fajans (1923) formulated rules governing covalent character in predominantly ionic bonds: high polarizing power of cation (high positive charge $z_+$, small radius $r_+$) and high polarizability of anion (large radius $r_-$, high negative charge $z_-$) maximize electron cloud distortion. Additionally, cations with pseudo-noble gas electron configurations ($18e^-$ outer shell, e.g. $Cu^+, Ag^+$) have higher polarizing power than noble gas ($8e^-$) cations due to poor $d$-electron shielding.

title: Mulliken Electronegativity Formula
formulaOrRule: \chi_M = \frac{IE + EA}{2} \text{ (eV)}, \quad \chi_P \approx 0.336(\chi_M - 0.615)
derivationOrExplanation: Robert Mulliken (1934) reasoned that an atom's tendency to attract electrons in a chemical bond depends on how difficult it is to remove an electron ($IE$) plus how strongly it attracts an incoming electron ($EA$). title: LCAO Approximation (Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals)
formulaOrRule: \psi_{MO} = c_A \phi_A \pm c_B \phi_B, \quad \psi_b = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2(1+S)}}(\phi_A + \phi_B), \quad \psi_a = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2(1-S)}}(\phi_A - \phi_B)
derivationOrExplanation: Approximate molecular wavefunction by linear superposition: $\psi = c_A \phi_A + c_B \phi_B$. Applying Rayleigh-Ritz variational method to minimize energy expectation value $E = \frac{\int \psi^* \hat{H} \psi dV}{\int \psi^* \psi dV}$ leads to secular determinant $\begin{vmatrix} H_{AA} - E & H_{AB} - E S \\ H_{BA} - E S & H_{BB} - E \end{vmatrix} = 0$. For homonuclear diatomic ($H_{AA} = H_{BB} = \alpha, H_{AB} = \beta$): roots are $E_b = \frac{\alpha + \beta}{1 + S}$ (bonding) and $E_a = \frac{\alpha - \beta}{1 - S}$ (antibonding).

title: Vector Addition of Bond Dipole Moments
formulaOrRule: \mu_{resultant} = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \mu_2^2 + 2\mu_1\mu_2\cos\theta}
derivationOrExplanation: Dipole moments are 3D vector quantities directed along bond axes. By vector law of cosines, resultant magnitude is $\mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \mu_2^2 + 2\mu_1\mu_2\cos\theta}$. For linear symmetric molecules ($\theta = 180^\circ$, e.g. $CO_2, BeF_2$), $\mu = \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$. For symmetric trigonal planar ($\theta = 120^\circ$, $BF_3$) and tetrahedral ($CH_4, CCl_4$), vector cancellation results in net $\mu = 0$.

title: Schomaker-Stevenson Equation for Heteronuclear Covalent Bond Length
formulaOrRule: d_{AB} = r_A + r_B - 0.09|\chi_A - \chi_B| \quad (\text{Schomaker-Stevenson Formula})
derivationOrExplanation: Simple additive covalent radii $d_{AB} = r_A + r_B$ overpredicts distances in polar bonds because partial ionic attraction pulls nuclei closer together. Schomaker and Stevenson (1941) introduced empirical correction proportional to electronegativity difference: $d_{AB} = r_A + r_B - c|\chi_A - \chi_B|$ where $c = 0.09\text{ \AA}$.

title: General Binomial Expansion for positive integer n
formulaOrRule: (x + y)^n = \sum_{r=0}^n \binom{n}{r} x^{n-r} y^r
derivationOrExplanation: By mathematical induction: Base case $n=1 \implies (x+y)^1 = \binom{1}{0}x + \binom{1}{1}y = x+y$. Inductive step: $(x+y)^{k+1} = (x+y)\sum_{r=0}^k \binom{k}{r}x^{k-r}y^r = \sum \binom{k}{r}x^{k-r+1}y^r + \sum \binom{k}{r}x^{k-r}y^{r+1}$. Shifting index and combining using Pascal identity $\binom{k}{r} + \binom{k}{r-1} = \binom{k+1}{r}$ yields $\sum_{r=0}^{k+1} \binom{k+1}{r} x^{k+1-r} y^r$.

title: Middle terms in binomial expansion
formulaOrRule: T_{middle} = \begin{cases} T_{\frac{n}{2} + 1} = \binom{n}{n/2} x^{n/2} y^{n/2} & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \\ T_{\frac{n+1}{2}} \text{ and } T_{\frac{n+3}{2}} & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \end{cases}
derivationOrExplanation: Total number of terms is $n+1$. If $n$ is even, $n+1$ is odd, so there is exactly one central term at index $\frac{(n+1)+1}{2} = \frac{n}{2} + 1$, corresponding to $r = n/2$. If $n$ is odd, $n+1$ is even, giving two central terms at positions $\frac{n+1}{2}$ and $\frac{n+3}{2}$ ($r = \frac{n-1}{2}$ and $r = \frac{n+1}{2}$).

title: Term independent of x (constant term)
formulaOrRule: T_{indep} = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r \quad \text{where } r = \frac{n p}{p + q} \text{ in } (a x^p + b x^{-q})^n

variablesOrTerms.r: integer value making net power of x zero
variablesOrTerms.p, q: powers of x in binomial terms

derivationOrExplanation: General term: $T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r}(ax^p)^{n-r}(bx^{-q})^r = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r x^{p(n-r) - qr}$. For the term to be independent of $x$, set exponent to zero: $pn - pr - qr = 0 \implies r(p+q) = np \implies r = \frac{np}{p+q}$. A constant term exists if and only if $r$ is an integer $0 \le r \le n$.

title: Numerically Greatest Term (NGT)
formulaOrRule: r = \left\lfloor \frac{(n + 1)|y|}{|x| + |y|} \right\rfloor \implies T_{r+1} \text{ is numerically greatest term in } (x + y)^n

variablesOrTerms.r: integer index for maximum absolute magnitude term

derivationOrExplanation: Consider ratio of consecutive terms: $\left|\frac{T_{r+1}}{T_r}\right| = \left|\frac{\binom{n}{r}x^{n-r}y^r}{\binom{n}{r-1}x^{n-r+1}y^{r-1}}\right| = \frac{n-r+1}{r}\left|\frac{y}{x}\right| \ge 1 \implies (n+1-r)|y| \ge r|x| \implies r(|x|+|y|) \le (n+1)|y| \implies r \le \frac{(n+1)|y|}{|x|+|y|}$.

title: Sum of all binomial coefficients
formulaOrRule: \sum_{r=0}^n \binom{n}{r} = C_0 + C_1 + C_2 + \dots + C_n = 2^n

variablesOrTerms.C_r: short-hand notation for binomial coefficient n choose r

derivationOrExplanation: Substitute $x = 1, y = 1$ into the binomial identity $(x + y)^n = \sum_{r=0}^n \binom{n}{r} x^{n-r} y^r$: $(1 + 1)^n = \sum_{r=0}^n \binom{n}{r} (1)^{n-r} (1)^r \implies 2^n = \sum_{r=0}^n C_r$.

title: Alternating sum of binomial coefficients
derivationOrExplanation: Substitute $x = 1, y = -1$ into $(x + y)^n$: $(1 - 1)^n = \sum_{r=0}^n \binom{n}{r} (1)^{n-r} (-1)^r = 0 \implies C_0 - C_1 + C_2 - C_3 + \dots = 0 \implies C_0 + C_2 + C_4 + \dots = C_1 + C_3 + C_5 + \dots = 2^{n-1}$.

title: Weighted sum of binomial coefficients
formulaOrRule: \sum_{r=1}^n r \binom{n}{r} = 1 C_1 + 2 C_2 + 3 C_3 + \dots + n C_n = n 2^{n-1}

title: Integral sum of reciprocal binomial coefficients
formulaOrRule: \sum_{r=0}^n \frac{\binom{n}{r}}{r + 1} = \frac{C_0}{1} + \frac{C_1}{2} + \dots + \frac{C_n}{n+1} = \frac{2^{n+1} - 1}{n + 1}
derivationOrExplanation: Integrate $(1+x)^n = \sum_{r=0}^n \binom{n}{r}x^r$ from $0$ to $1$: $\int_0^1 (1+x)^n dx = \sum_{r=0}^n C_r \int_0^1 x^r dx \implies \left[\frac{(1+x)^{n+1}}{n+1}\right]_0^1 = \sum_{r=0}^n \frac{C_r}{r+1} \implies \frac{2^{n+1} - 1}{n+1} = \sum_{r=0}^n \frac{C_r}{r+1}$.

title: Sum of squares of binomial coefficients
derivationOrExplanation: Consider $(1+x)^n(x+1)^n = (1+x)^{2n}$. Left side expansion: $(C_0 + C_1 x + \dots + C_n x^n)(C_0 x^n + C_1 x^{n-1} + \dots + C_n)$. The coefficient of $x^n$ is $C_0^2 + C_1^2 + \dots + C_n^2$. On the right side $(1+x)^{2n}$, the coefficient of $x^n$ is $\binom{2n}{n}$. Equating gives $\sum C_r^2 = \binom{2n}{n}$.

flashcard.back:

title: Vandermonde's Convolution Identity
formulaOrRule: \sum_{k=0}^r \binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{r - k} = \binom{m + n}{r}
derivationOrExplanation: Equating coefficient of $x^r$ on both sides of $(1+x)^m (1+x)^n = (1+x)^{m+n}$. On LHS: $\left(\sum_{k=0}^m \binom{m}{k}x^k\right)\left(\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}x^j\right)$. Setting $j = r-k$ collects terms of power $x^r$: $\sum_{k=0}^r \binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{r-k}$. On RHS, the coefficient of $x^r$ is $\binom{m+n}{r}$.

title: Multinomial Theorem Expansion
formulaOrRule: (x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_k)^n = \sum_{r_1 + r_2 + \dots + r_k = n} \frac{n!}{r_1! r_2! \dots r_k!} x_1^{r_1} x_2^{r_2} \dots x_k^{r_k}

variablesOrTerms.k: number of terms in base polynomial

derivationOrExplanation: Expand product of $n$ identical factors $(x_1 + \dots + x_k)$. Each term in the expanded polynomial is formed by choosing $x_1$ from $r_1$ factors, $x_2$ from $r_2$ factors, ..., and $x_k$ from $r_k$ factors where $\sum r_i = n$. The number of ways to choose these factors is given by the multinomial coefficient $\binom{n}{r_1, r_2, \dots, r_k} = \frac{n!}{r_1! r_2! \dots r_k!}$.

(x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_k)^n = \sum_{r_1 + r_2 + \dots + r_k = n} \frac{n!}{r_1! r_2! \dots r_k!} x_1^{r_1} x_2^{r_2} \dots x_k^{r_k}

title: Binomial Expansion for Any Rational Index n
derivationOrExplanation: Using Maclaurin series expansion of $f(x) = (1+x)^n$: $f(0) = 1$, $f'(0) = n$, $f''(0) = n(n-1)$, $f^{(k)}(0) = n(n-1)\dots(n-k+1)$. By Taylor theorem: $f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!} x^k = 1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2 + \dots$ By the ratio test, $\lim \left|\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}\right| = \lim \left|\frac{n-k}{k+1}x\right| = |x| < 1$ for convergence.

flashcard.front: What is Binomial Expansion for Any Rational Index n?
flashcard.back:
(1 + x)^n = 1 + n x + \frac{n(n - 1)}{2!} x^2 + \frac{n(n - 1)(n - 2)}{3!} x^3 + \dots \quad (|x| < 1)

title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction and Lenz's Law
formulaOrRule: \mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = -N\frac{d}{dt}\left(\int \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A}\right)
derivationOrExplanation: Empirical discovery by Michael Faraday (1831). The negative sign (Lenz's Law, Heinrich Lenz 1834) enforces energy conservation: the induced current flows in such a direction that its own magnetic field opposes the original flux change that produced it.

title: Motional EMF in a Moving Conductor
formulaOrRule: \mathcal{E}_{motional} = B v l \sin\theta = (\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{l}
derivationOrExplanation: Mobile conduction electrons inside rod experience magnetic Lorentz force $\vec{F}_B = -e(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. Work done moving an electron through length $\vec{l}$ is $W = \int \vec{F}_B \cdot d\vec{l} = -e \int (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot d\vec{l}$. Induced EMF is work done per unit positive charge: $\mathcal{E} = W/(-e) = (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{l} = B v l\sin\theta$.

title: Rotational Motional EMF of a Rotating Rod
formulaOrRule: \mathcal{E}_{rot} = \frac{1}{2}B \omega l^2
derivationOrExplanation: Consider element $dr$ at distance $r$ from pivot: linear velocity is $v(r) = r\omega$. Motional EMF generated across element is $d\mathcal{E} = B v(r) dr = B(r\omega)dr$. Integrating from pivot $r=0$ to tip $r=l$: $\mathcal{E} = B\omega \int_0^l r dr = B\omega \left[\frac{r^2}{2}\right]_0^l = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.

title: Self-Inductance and Magnetic Energy Density
formulaOrRule: L = \frac{N \Phi_B}{I} = \mu_0 n^2 A l, \quad U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I^2, \quad u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}
derivationOrExplanation: Inside solenoid, field is $B = \mu_0 n I$. Flux per turn is $\Phi = B A = \mu_0 n I A$. Total linkage is $\lambda = N\Phi = (nl)(\mu_0 n I A) = (\mu_0 n^2 A l)I$. By definition $L = \lambda / I = \mu_0 n^2 A l$. Work required to establish current $I$ against back-EMF $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{di}{dt}$ is $U = \int P\,dt = \int (L\frac{di}{dt} i)dt = L \int_0^I i\,di = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$. Dividing by volume $V = Al$ and using $B = \mu_0 n I$ yields $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$.

title: Mutual Inductance and Coupling Coefficient
formulaOrRule: M = \frac{N_2 \Phi_{21}}{I_1} = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l, \quad M \le \sqrt{L_1 L_2}
derivationOrExplanation: Current $I_1$ in outer coil produces uniform field $B_1 = \mu_0 n_1 I_1$. Flux passing through each turn of inner coil of area $A$ is $\Phi_{21} = B_1 A = \mu_0 n_1 I_1 A$. Total linkage with coil 2 ($N_2 = n_2 l$ turns) is $\lambda_2 = N_2 \Phi_{21} = (n_2 l)(\mu_0 n_1 I_1 A) = (\mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l)I_1$. Mutual inductance is $M = \lambda_2 / I_1 = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l$. By reciprocity theorem, $M_{12} = M_{21} = M$.

title: Transient LR Circuit Growth and Decay
formulaOrRule: i(t) = I_0 (1 - e^{-t / \tau_L}) \quad (\text{Growth}), \quad i(t) = I_0 e^{-t / \tau_L} \quad (\text{Decay}), \quad \tau_L = \frac{L}{R}
derivationOrExplanation: KVL during growth: $\mathcal{E} - L\frac{di}{dt} - iR = 0 \implies L\frac{di}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - iR$. Separating variables: $\frac{di}{\mathcal{E} - iR} = \frac{dt}{L}$. Integrating with $i(0) = 0$: $-\frac{1}{R}\ln\left(1 - \frac{iR}{\mathcal{E}}\right) = \frac{t}{L} \implies i(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right)$.

title: Root-Mean-Square (RMS) Values of Sinusoidal AC
formulaOrRule: V_{rms} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707 V_0, \quad I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707 I_0
derivationOrExplanation: For $i(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t)$, Joule heat generated in resistor $R$ over one period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ is $H = \int_0^T i^2(t) R dt$. An equivalent DC current $I_{rms}$ dissipates identical heat: $I_{rms}^2 R T = R \int_0^T I_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t) dt$. Since the average of $\sin^2(\omega t)$ over full period is $\frac{1}{2}$: $I_{rms}^2 T = I_0^2 \left(\frac{T}{2}\right) \implies I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$.

derivationOrExplanation: Phasor analysis: current phasor $\tilde{I}$ is common in series loop. Resistor voltage $\tilde{V}_R = I R$ is in phase with current. Inductor voltage $\tilde{V}_L = I X_L$ leads current by $+90^\circ (+i)$. Capacitor voltage $\tilde{V}_C = I X_C$ lags current by $-90^\circ (-i)$. Total complex voltage is $\tilde{V} = \tilde{V}_R + \tilde{V}_L + \tilde{V}_C = I [R + i(X_L - X_C)]$. Impedance magnitude is $Z = |\tilde{V}|/I = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor (Q) of Series LCR
formulaOrRule: \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}, \quad Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}
derivationOrExplanation: Current amplitude is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}}$. Current is maximized when reactive term vanishes: $\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = 0 \implies \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC} \implies \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance, impedance is purely resistive ($Z_{min} = R$) and current is in phase with voltage ($\cos\phi = 1$). Quality factor is $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$ where $\Delta\omega$ is bandwidth at half-power points.

title: Average AC Power and Power Factor
formulaOrRule: P_{avg} = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi, \quad \text{Power Factor} = \cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}
derivationOrExplanation: Instantaneous power is $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = [V_0 \sin(\omega t)][I_0 \sin(\omega t - \phi)] = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)[\sin\omega t\cos\phi - \cos\omega t\sin\phi] = V_0 I_0 [\sin^2\omega t\cos\phi - \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi]$. Averaging over a full cycle: $\langle \sin^2\omega t \rangle = 1/2$ and $\langle \sin\omega t\cos\omega t \rangle = 0$. Hence $P_{avg} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$. From impedance triangle, $\cos\phi = R/Z$.

title: Ideal Transformer Voltage, Current and Turns Ratio
formulaOrRule: \frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = \frac{I_p}{I_s} = k, \quad \eta = \frac{V_s I_s}{V_p I_p} \times 100\%
derivationOrExplanation: Assuming ideal core with zero flux leakage: common flux $\Phi$ links both windings. Induced EMFs are $V_p = -N_p \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $V_s = -N_s \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. Dividing gives $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$. For an ideal lossless transformer (100% efficiency), input power equals output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s \implies \frac{I_p}{I_s} = \frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$.

title: LC Tank Circuit Oscillations
formulaOrRule: \omega_{LC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad q(t) = Q_0 \cos(\omega_{LC} t), \quad i(t) = -\omega_{LC} Q_0 \sin(\omega_{LC} t)
derivationOrExplanation: Total circuit energy is $E = U_E + U_B = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}Li^2$. In lossless circuit, $\frac{dE}{dt} = 0$: $\frac{q}{C}\frac{dq}{dt} + L i \frac{di}{dt} = 0$. Since $i = \frac{dq}{dt}$, dividing by $i$ gives $\frac{q}{C} + L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} = 0 \implies \frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0$. This is standard SHM equation with $\omega_{LC} = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. Solution with initial charge $Q_0$ is $q(t) = Q_0\cos(\omega t)$.

title: Maxwell's Displacement Current
formulaOrRule: I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = \epsilon_0 A \frac{dE}{dt}
derivationOrExplanation: Between capacitor plates during charging, no conduction electrons flow, yet magnetic field exists. Electric field is $E = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A} \implies Q = \epsilon_0 E A = \epsilon_0 \Phi_E$. Differentiating charge with respect to time: $I_c = \frac{dQ}{dt} = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$. Maxwell recognized this time-varying flux term acts as an effective displacement current $I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$, restoring Ampere's law to $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (I_c + I_d)$.

title: Integration by Parts Formula
formulaOrRule: \int u \, v \, dx = u \int v \, dx - \int \left( u' \int v \, dx \right) dx

variablesOrTerms.u: differentiable function chosen via ILATE rule

derivationOrExplanation: Differentiating the product of two functions: $\frac{d}{dx}[u \cdot w] = u' w + u w'$. Integrating both sides: $u w = \int u' w dx + \int u w' dx \implies \int u w' dx = u w - \int u' w dx$. Let $v = w' \implies w = \int v dx$. Substituting $w$: $\int u v dx = u \int v dx - \int \left(u' \int v dx\right) dx$.

title: King's Property of Definite Integrals
formulaOrRule: \int_a^b f(x) \, dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x) \, dx \quad (\text{King's Property})
derivationOrExplanation: Substitute $t = a + b - x \implies dx = -dt$. When $x = a$, $t = b$; when $x = b$, $t = a$. $\int_a^b f(x) dx = \int_b^a f(a + b - t)(-dt) = \int_a^b f(a + b - t) dt = \int_a^b f(a + b - x) dx$.

title: Queen's Property for Definite Integrals
formulaOrRule: \int_0^{2a} f(x) \, dx = \begin{cases} 2 \int_0^a f(x) \, dx & \text{if } f(2a - x) = f(x) \\ 0 & \text{if } f(2a - x) = -f(x) \end{cases} \quad (\text{Queen's Property})
derivationOrExplanation: Split the integral: $\int_0^{2a} f(x) dx = \int_0^a f(x) dx + \int_a^{2a} f(x) dx$. In the second integral, substitute $x = 2a - t \implies dx = -dt$: $\int_a^{2a} f(x) dx = \int_a^0 f(2a - t)(-dt) = \int_0^a f(2a - t) dt = \int_0^a f(2a - x) dx$. Thus $\int_0^{2a} f(x) dx = \int_0^a [f(x) + f(2a - x)] dx$. If $f(2a-x) = f(x)$, sum is $2\int_0^a f(x) dx$. If $f(2a-x) = -f(x)$, sum is $0$.

title: Symmetry Integral for Even and Odd Functions
formulaOrRule: \int_{-a}^a f(x) \, dx = \begin{cases} 2 \int_0^a f(x) \, dx & \text{if } f(-x) = f(x) \text{ (even)} \\ 0 & \text{if } f(-x) = -f(x) \text{ (odd)} \end{cases}
derivationOrExplanation: Split: $\int_{-a}^a f(x) dx = \int_{-a}^0 f(x) dx + \int_0^a f(x) dx$. In the first integral, substitute $x = -t \implies dx = -dt$: $\int_{-a}^0 f(x) dx = \int_a^0 f(-t)(-dt) = \int_0^a f(-t) dt = \int_0^a f(-x) dx$. Hence $\int_{-a}^a f(x) dx = \int_0^a [f(x) + f(-x)] dx$. If $f$ is even ($f(-x) = f(x)$), sum is $2\int_0^a f(x) dx$. If $f$ is odd ($f(-x) = -f(x)$), integrand cancels to $0$.

title: Leibniz Rule for Differentiation Under the Integral Sign
formulaOrRule: \frac{d}{dx}\left[ \int_{u(x)}^{v(x)} f(x, t) \, dt \right] = f(x, v(x)) v'(x) - f(x, u(x)) u'(x) + \int_{u(x)}^{v(x)} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, t) \, dt
derivationOrExplanation: Let $F(x, u, v) = \int_u^v f(x, t) dt$. By multivariable chain rule: $\frac{dF}{dx} = \frac{\partial F}{\partial v} \frac{dv}{dx} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial u} \frac{du}{dx} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}$. By Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: $\frac{\partial F}{\partial v} = f(x, v)$ and $\frac{\partial F}{\partial u} = -f(x, u)$. Differentiating under integral gives $\frac{\partial F}{\partial x} = \int_u^v \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} dt$. Combining yields the full Leibniz differentiation formula.

title: Limit of a Sum as a Definite Integral (Riemann Sum)
formulaOrRule: \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=1}^n f\left(\frac{r}{n}\right) = \int_0^1 f(x) \, dx
derivationOrExplanation: Partition interval $[0, 1]$ into $n$ equal subintervals of width $\Delta x = 1/n$. The right endpoint of the $r$-th subinterval is $x_r = r/n$. The Riemann sum is $\sum_{r=1}^n f(x_r) \Delta x = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=1}^n f(r/n)$. As $n \to \infty$, $\Delta x \to 0$. By definition of the Riemann integral for continuous functions, this sum converges to $\int_0^1 f(x) dx$.

title: Exponential Derivative Cancellation Integral
formulaOrRule: \int e^x [f(x) + f'(x)] \, dx = e^x f(x) + C
derivationOrExplanation: Expand into two integrals: $\int e^x f(x) dx + \int e^x f'(x) dx$. Integrate the first integral by parts, choosing $u = f(x)$ and $v = e^x$: $\int e^x f(x) dx = f(x) e^x - \int f'(x) e^x dx$. Substituting back: $\left[f(x) e^x - \int f'(x) e^x dx\right] + \int e^x f'(x) dx = e^x f(x) + C$. The second integral cancels out completely.

title: Wallis' Formula for Powers of Sine and Cosine
formulaOrRule: \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n x \, dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^n x \, dx = \begin{cases} \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot \frac{n-3}{n-2} \dots \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \\ \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot \frac{n-3}{n-2} \dots \frac{2}{3} \cdot 1 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \end{cases}
derivationOrExplanation: Let $I_n = \int_0^{\\pi/2} \sin^n x dx = \int_0^{\\pi/2} \sin^{n-1} x \sin x dx$. Integrate by parts with $u = \sin^{n-1} x, dv = \sin x dx \implies v = -\cos x$: $I_n = [-\sin^{n-1} x \cos x]_0^{\\pi/2} + (n-1)\int_0^{\\pi/2} \sin^{n-2} x \cos^2 x dx = 0 + (n-1)\int_0^{\\pi/2} \sin^{n-2} x (1 - \sin^2 x) dx = (n-1)I_{n-2} - (n-1)I_n \implies n I_n = (n-1)I_{n-2} \implies I_n = \frac{n-1}{n} I_{n-2}$. Repeated application down to $I_0 = \pi/2$ or $I_1 = 1$ yields Wallis' formula.

formulaOrRule: \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 \pm a^2}} = \ln|x + \sqrt{x^2 \pm a^2}| + C

For $-a^2$: substitute $x = a\sec\theta$.

title: Area Enclosed Between Two Curves
formulaOrRule: A = \int_a^b |f(x) - g(x)| \, dx
derivationOrExplanation: Partition $[a, b]$ into $n$ vertical strips of width $\Delta x$. The height of the strip at point $x_i$ is $|f(x_i) - g(x_i)|$. Area of strip is $|f(x_i) - g(x_i)| \Delta x$. Summing areas across all strips: $A = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^n |f(x_i) - g(x_i)| \Delta x = \int_a^b |f(x) - g(x)| dx$. If $f(x) \ge g(x)$ throughout $[a, b]$, absolute value simplifies to $\int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)] dx$.

title: Volume of Solid of Revolution (Disk Method)
formulaOrRule: V = \pi \int_a^b [f(x)]^2 \, dx

derivationOrExplanation: Slice the solid of revolution perpendicular to x-axis into thin circular disks of thickness $dx$. Integrating from $x = a$ to $x = b$ sums the volumes of all disks: $V = \pi \int_a^b [f(x)]^2 dx$.

formulaOrRule: \vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}, \quad U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}

title: Transient Response of RC Circuit
formulaOrRule: q(t) = Q_0 (1 - e^{-t / RC}) \quad (\text{Charging}), \quad q(t) = Q_0 e^{-t / RC} \quad (\text{Discharging})
derivationOrExplanation: Kirchhoff loop during charging: $\mathcal{E} - iR - \frac{q}{C} = 0$. Using $i = \frac{dq}{dt}$: $R\frac{dq}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - \frac{q}{C} = \frac{C\mathcal{E} - q}{C}$. title: Capacitance of Spherical Capacitors
formulaOrRule: C_{spherical} = 4\pi\epsilon_0 \frac{a b}{b - a}, \quad C_{isolated} = 4\pi\epsilon_0 R
derivationOrExplanation: Concentric shells with charges $+Q$ and $-Q$: field between shells is $E(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$. Potential difference is $V = \int_a^b E(r)dr = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{b}\right) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{b-a}{ab}\right)$. Capacitance $C = \frac{Q}{V} = 4\pi\epsilon_0 \frac{ab}{b-a}$. For isolated single sphere, set outer radius $b \to \infty$: $C = 4\pi\epsilon_0 a$.

title: Torque and Angular Momentum Equation
formulaOrRule: \vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = I\vec{\alpha} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}
derivationOrExplanation: Angular momentum is $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$. Differentiating: $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p} + \vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{v} \times (m\vec{v}) + \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_{net} = 0 + \vec{\tau}_{net}$. For rigid bodies rotating about fixed axis, $\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega}$, so $\vec{\tau} = I\frac{d\vec{\omega}}{dt} = I\vec{\alpha}$.

title: Parallel Axis Theorem (Steiner's Theorem)
formulaOrRule: I_{parallel} = I_{cm} + M d^2

variablesOrTerms.I_{cm}: Moment of inertia about parallel axis through center of mass
variablesOrTerms.I_{parallel}: Moment of inertia about arbitrary parallel axis

derivationOrExplanation: Let origin be CM. Coordinate along new axis is $(x + d, y)$. Then $I = \int [(x+d)^2 + y^2] dm = \int (x^2 + y^2) dm + 2d \int x dm + d^2 \int dm$. Since origin is CM, first moment $\int x dm = 0$. Hence $I = I_{cm} + Md^2$.

title: Perpendicular Axis Theorem
formulaOrRule: I_z = I_x + I_y

variablesOrTerms.I_z: Moment of inertia about axis perpendicular to lamina plane

title: Center of Mass Velocity and Koenig's Theorem for Angular Momentum
formulaOrRule: v_c = \frac{m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \quad L_O = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{L}_{cm}
derivationOrExplanation: Let $\vec{r}_i = \vec{r}_{cm} + \vec{r}'_i$ and $\vec{v}_i = \vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{v}'_i$. Total angular momentum $\vec{L}_O = \sum m_i (\vec{r}_{cm} + \vec{r}'_i) \times (\vec{v}_{cm} + \vec{v}'_i) = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + \sum m_i \vec{r}'_i \times \vec{v}'_i + \vec{r}_{cm} \times \sum m_i \vec{v}'_i + (\sum m_i \vec{r}'_i) \times \vec{v}_{cm}$. By definition of CM, cross terms vanish, giving $\vec{L}_O = \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm} + I_{cm}\vec{\omega}$.

flashcard.back:

title: Condition for Toppling Before Sliding
formulaOrRule: h_{topple} = \frac{b}{2\mu} \quad (\text{or } \mu > b/h)

variablesOrTerms.\\mu: Coefficient of friction between block and floor

derivationOrExplanation: Let horizontal force $F$ be applied at top height $h$. Sliding occurs when $F = \mu mg$. Toppling occurs about front edge when overturning torque exceeds stabilizing torque: $F h > mg (b/2) \implies F > mg \frac{b}{2h}$. Toppling occurs prior to sliding if $F_{topple} < F_{slide} \implies mg \frac{b}{2h} < \mu mg \implies \mu > \frac{b}{2h}$.

title: Time Period of Physical (Compound) Pendulum
formulaOrRule: T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{I}{m g d}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{k^2 + d^2}{g d}}
derivationOrExplanation: Restoring torque about pivot for deflection $\theta$ is $\tau = -mgd\sin\theta \approx -mgd\theta$. title: Bayes' Theorem for Conditional Posterior Probability
formulaOrRule: P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)}
derivationOrExplanation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(E_i | A) = \frac{P(E_i \cap A)}{P(A)} = \frac{P(E_i) P(A | E_i)}{P(A)}$. By the Law of Total Probability, since $E_1, \dots, E_n$ partition the sample space $S$: $A = A \cap S = A \cap (\bigcup E_j) = \bigcup (A \cap E_j)$. Since $E_j$ are mutually disjoint: $P(A) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(A \cap E_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n P(E_j) P(A | E_j)$. Substituting $P(A)$ yields Bayes' theorem.

subject: Mathematics
title: Binomial Distribution Probability Mass Function, Mean and Variance
formulaOrRule: P(X = r) = \binom{n}{r} p^r q^{n - r} \quad (q = 1 - p), \quad \mu = n p, \quad \sigma^2 = n p q
derivationOrExplanation: In $n$ independent trials, the probability of any specific sequence with $r$ successes and $n-r$ failures is $p^r q^{n-r}$. The number of distinct sequences is the combinations of choosing $r$ trials out of $n$: $\binom{n}{r}$. Hence $P(X = r) = \binom{n}{r} p^r q^{n-r}$. Expectation: $E[X] = \sum r \binom{n}{r} p^r q^{n-r} = n p \sum \binom{n-1}{r-1} p^{r-1} q^{(n-1)-(r-1)} = n p (p+q)^{n-1} = n p$. Variance: $\text{Var}(X) = E[X(X-1)] + E[X] - (E[X])^2 = n(n-1)p^2 + np - n^2 p^2 = np(1-p) = npq$.

subject: Mathematics
title: Addition Theorem of Probability
formulaOrRule: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)

variablesOrTerms.P(A \\cup B): probability of occurrence of at least one event

derivationOrExplanation: From set theory cardinality: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. Dividing both sides by the total number of outcomes in the finite sample space $n(S)$: $\frac{n(A \cup B)}{n(S)} = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)} + \frac{n(B)}{n(S)} - \frac{n(A \cap B)}{n(S)} \implies P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$. If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive ($A \cap B = \emptyset$), $P(A \cap B) = 0 \implies P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.

subject: Mathematics
title: Condition for Independence of Two Events
formulaOrRule: P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B) \iff A, B \text{ are Independent}
derivationOrExplanation: By definition of conditional probability: $P(A | B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$. Two events are independent if the occurrence of event $B$ has no influence on the probability of event $A$: $P(A | B) = P(A)$. Equating: $P(A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \implies P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B)$.

title: Expectation and Variance of a Discrete Random Variable
formulaOrRule: E[X] = \mu = \sum x_i P(x_i), \quad \text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = \sum (x_i - \mu)^2 P(x_i)

title: Effect of Linear Transformation on Mean and Variance
formulaOrRule: E[a X + b] = a E[X] + b, \quad \text{Var}(a X + b) = a^2 \text{Var}(X), \quad \sigma_{aX+b} = |a| \sigma_X
